description: Growth scare. Equities fall 20%; Treasuries rally 5% on a flight to quality; commodities soften 5% on weaker demand; REITs fall 18%, tracking equities but cushioned slightly by the duration rally. Coherent because the same shock drives all four legs: a downgrade to growth expectations is bad for equities and real assets and good for duration.

Hawkish repricing of the curve. Long Treasuries fall 30% (200bp against ~17-year duration); equities fall 8% through the discount rate rather than through earnings; commodities are unchanged because the shock is monetary, not a demand event; REITs fall 12%, worse than equities, because they carry both duration and financing-cost sensitivity. Coherent as a policy shock with no growth downgrade attached.

Global demand shock. Commodities fall 30%; equities fall 10%; duration rallies 6% as the disinflationary impulse is priced in; REITs fall 8%, the mildest real-asset leg because lower rates partly offset weaker growth. Coherent: falling commodities and rallying bonds are the standard joint signature of a demand-driven slowdown.

Moves are moderate (equities -12%, REITs -12%, commodities -10%, duration +4%) but pairwise correlations converge to 0.90, so the damage comes from diversification failing rather than from any one leg.

Equities -25% and duration -20% fall together, so bonds stop hedging equities; commodities RISE 15%, which is the feature that makes this stagflation rather than a generic sell-off, and the reason it is the worst scenario for the 60/40 benchmark specifically.

A forced-liquidation event, not an economic one. Equities -30%, duration -25%, commodities -20%, REITs -35%, correlations at 0.95. Rates rising WHILE commodities collapse is not an inflation story and would be incoherent as a macro forecast; it is the signature of a dash for cash, where leveraged holders sell whatever is liquid and everything falls together except cash. The week of 9-20 March 2020 is the precedent: equities, Treasuries and gold all sold off at once. This is also the scenario where the framework's lack of any liquidity modelling bites hardest, since a real liquidation event widens spreads and the losses here assume none of that. Hypothetical stress assumptions, not forecasts.
